name: Jon Eric McPike
title: Jon Eric McPike: Worst to First, and After
dek: He turned the worst-performing rehabilitation hospital in a national system into its best, built companies with his wife, lost them, and came back with three numbers.
excerpt: Jon Eric McPike spent nearly four decades in healthcare, from a failing hospital turned top performer to companies built and lost. Out of the loss came The 3.2.1. Experience.
seoDescription: Jon Eric McPike on worst to first, losing his companies, and the 3.2.1. method: three gratitudes, two intentions, one bold action.
content:
Jon Eric McPike was put in charge days after he finished high school. He was young and short on experience, and by his own account he was lucky twice over: in his mentors, and in the caregivers he was sent to lead. Then came individual facilities, regional roles, then hospital leadership, and eventually businesses of his own. Nearly four decades in healthcare later, he is Senior Healthcare Consultant at Remarkable Unlimited and the creator of The Leadership Superpower Matrix.

His first major crisis came on a Saturday morning, with a call that one patient had killed another using the drawer from his bedside table. He drove in. He and the Director of Nursing assessed the situation and within minutes had a plan. Then he walked the building and checked on every employee, one at a time. Do you feel safe? Are you okay? What do you need right now? Before you can stabilize the organization, he says, you have to help stabilize the people.

Worst to first

Later he agreed to become CEO of what was considered the worst-performing rehabilitation hospital in a national system. He did not replace the leadership team. He believed in the people who were already there. The hospital became the top performer on virtually every major measure: patient satisfaction, employee satisfaction, volume, financial performance and regulatory outcomes, including the best licensure survey in the company. What he remembers is not the scorecard. It is employees who had given years to the place beginning to believe in themselves again.

With his wife he then built healthcare businesses that grew to $27 million in annual revenue. During COVID their facilities became COVID treatment centers, and among the COVID patients they treated the recovery rate was 96 percent. There was bankruptcy, litigation and a long fight against organizations with far deeper financial resources. They lost anyway. Sometimes in business, he says, determination alone isn't enough.

Three, two, one

The loss took years of work, a great deal of money and a piece of his identity. To quiet his thoughts he played Solitaire on his phone, and for nearly a month he could not get the 3, 2 and Ace he needed to finish a game. He started repeating a mantra to himself. Then, sitting in a U-Haul truck while preparing to move the office in South Texas, he knew what 3.2.1. meant, and typed it as fast as he could: three gratitudes, two intentions, one bold action.

He read into the neuroscience of gratitude, neuroplasticity and habit formation, not to write a book but to find his own way forward. The reframe that changed things was a question. What if what he went through was not only a loss, but also an education? The book, The 3.2.1. Experience, came after. So did the keynotes.

Systems and people

As a consultant, he starts with understanding before changing: the culture, the people, the processes, and then the financial and operational results. The numbers tell him where to look. The aim is twofold: specific, measurable action plans that a team can execute after the engagement ends, and momentum within the workforce, which is where the 3.2.1. principles come in. Successful transformation, in his view, needs better systems and engaged people. The Leadership Superpower Matrix adds a third tool, a set of four leadership quadrants and a brief assessment that help leaders know their own strengths, understand those of the people around them and build teams around both.

With Laurie Beth McPike he has written more than 20 Cowboy Kyler adventures for children. He was named an Author of the Year Finalist for Rusty's Farewell. The follow-up book, The 3.2.1. Experience: The Middle Rounds, is about the stretch where progress slows and doubt creeps in. What he hopes people take from all of it is one word. Hope that change is possible, and that today's circumstances don't define tomorrow.
